text: When you launch a server in the cloud, it doesn't just float out in the open internet. It lives inside a virtual network: an isolated, software-defined slice of network space that you create and control, even though the physical routers and switches underneath belong to the cloud provider and are shared across thousands of other customers at the same time.

AWS calls this a VPC, short for Virtual Private Cloud. Azure calls the exact same concept a VNet, short for Virtual Network. Different vendors, different names, same underlying job: give you a private IP address range that nothing outside your account can see or touch unless you explicitly allow it. This is exactly where everything you learned earlier about IP addressing, subnetting, and routing actually gets applied, just inside a cloud provider's infrastructure instead of on physical hardware you own and rack yourself.

When you create a VPC or VNet, you choose its address range in CIDR notation, something like 10.0.0.0/16, which gives you roughly sixty-five thousand private addresses to work with. That range belongs to you alone. Two completely unrelated companies can both pick that exact same range for their own networks and never interfere with each other, because each VPC or VNet is its own walled-off network namespace, invisible to every other customer on the same shared hardware.

A brand-new VPC or VNet starts out isolated by default: nothing inside can reach the public internet and nothing on the internet can reach in, until you deliberately open a path, like an internet gateway, a NAT gateway, or a VPN connection. Isolation is the safe starting point, not an inconvenience. Everything you create afterward — virtual machines, databases, load balancers — gets placed inside that network and draws a private address from the range you defined up front.

Next lesson: subnets, routing tables, and security groups — how you carve that VPC or VNet into smaller, more tightly controlled pieces instead of leaving the whole thing as one flat, undivided address space.
